lesson.title: qui & que
lesson.subtitle: Relative pronouns qui (subject), que (object), and dont ('of which') — welding two sentences into one

hook.title: How French Welds Sentences Without Looking at Human vs. Thing
hook.content: In English, choosing between 'who' and 'which' depends on whether you are talking about a person or a thing ('the man WHO speaks' vs. 'the train WHICH leaves'). French doesn't care at all whether the noun is a person or a train! Instead, French looks purely at the GRAMMATICAL JOB right after the weld: if the next word is the VERB (missing its subject), use qui ('the man who speaks' = l'homme qui parle; 'the train which arrives' = le train qui arrive). If the next word is a SUBJECT PRONOUN or NOUN (missing its object), use que ('the coffee that I want' = le café que je veux)!

footnotes.title: The golden shortcut: qui + verb vs. que (qu') + subject
footnotes.content: Look one word to the right of the gap: is there a subject (je, tu, il, Marie) right after it? If yes, use que (elided to qu' before a vowel: le film qu'il aime)! Is the verb standing right there with no subject? Use qui (which NEVER elides, even before a vowel: l'homme qui arrive)!

pattern.title: Never Drop 'That' in French — and Meet dont ('of which')
pattern.content: In English you can drop 'that' whenever you feel like it ('the coffee [that] I want'). In French, you can NEVER drop que: le café que je veux is mandatory! And what if the verb normally uses de (like parler de 'to talk about' or avoir besoin de 'to have need of')? Then de + relative fuses into the single sleek word dont: C'est le livre dont je parle ('That's the book I'm talking about / of which I speak').
pattern.linguist_note: Latin nominative quī (subject) and accusative quem/quid (object) preserved their case distinction in French qui vs. que across both animate and inanimate antecedents.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: dropping que like English drops 'that' (*le café je veux) or eliding qui before a vowel (*l'homme qu'arrive). Never drop que, and never elide qui!

exercises.prompt: Match each relative pronoun with the grammatical slot that follows it:

matching_pairs.german: Followed directly by the verb (subject of clause)
Followed by a subject + verb (object of clause)
Used when the verb or noun takes de (parler de)

exercises.target_answer: Followed directly by the verb (subject of clause), Followed by a subject + verb (object of clause), Used when the verb or noun takes de (parler de), Where / when (la ville où j'habite)
exercises.meaning: qui (never elides!), que / qu' (never omitted!), dont (replaces de + relative), où (place or time relative)
exercises.explanation: French chooses qui vs. que by grammatical role (subject vs. object), not human vs. thing.

exercises.prompt: Fill the two blanks: 'Le train ___ arrive est rapide' ('The train that is arriving is fast').
options: Le train que arrive est rapide
Le train qui arrive est rapide
exercises.target_answer: Le train qui arrive est rapide
exercises.meaning: The train that arrives is fast
exercises.explanation: Because the verb arrive comes immediately after the gap (it needs a subject), use qui — and qui NEVER elides before a vowel!

exercises.prompt: Fill the weld: 'La table ___ j'ai réservée' ('The table [that] I reserved').
exercises.explanation: A subject (j') follows the gap, so the missing piece is the object → que (never omitted in French!).

exercises.idea: the man who is speaking is my father
cues: The man who speaks → L'homme qui parle + is my father → est mon père
idea_parts: head noun + subject relative → L'homme qui parle
main verb + complement → est mon père
exercises.target_answer: L'homme qui parle est mon père
exercises.meaning: The man who is speaking is my father
exercises.explanation: parle has no other subject, so qui bridges L'homme to parle.

diagnosis.slip: used que instead of qui before the verb
diagnosis.cue: Before a verb lacking a subject, always use qui.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: C'est le livre dont je parle
exercises.target_answer: C'est le livre dont je parle
exercises.meaning: That is the book I am talking about
cues: of-which I speak: dont je parle
exercises.explanation: Because French says parler DE quelque chose, 'the book that I speak OF' uses dont.
exercises.affirmation: You caught dont before je parle.

summary.outcome: Link clauses using qui (before a verb), que/qu' (before a subject), and dont (for de-constructions).

use_example.german: La ville où j'habite et le café que j'aime.
use_example.english: The city where I live and the café that I love.

summary.takeaway: qui + verb, que + subject, dont for de — and never leave 'that' out.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2801] The Man That Knows): see how qui & que leads directly into The Man That Knows.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'The coffee that I want is here':
twist.target_answer: Le café que je veux est ici
twist.explanation: que connects le café (the object wanted) to je veux.

foreshadow.line: Having mastered qui & que, look ahead to Topic 29 (The French Mind), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 27 (il faut) now pays off directly inside qui & que: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

qui.context_phrase: L'homme qui parle est mon père.
qui.context_translation: The man who is speaking is my father.
qui.etymology_derivation: Followed directly by the verb. Never drops its i before a vowel!

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

dont.context_phrase: C'est le film dont je parle.
dont.context_translation: That's the film I'm talking about (lit. of which I speak).
dont.etymology_derivation: Whenever the verb takes de (parler de, avoir besoin de), French uses dont.

où.etymology_derivation: Latin ubi 'where' — the root English borrowed wholesale in 'ubiquitous' (present everywhere).

homme.etymology_derivation: Latin homō 'man' — the root of human, homicide, humus (of the earth). The H is written and never said.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

voir.context_translation: I'm going to see my friend.
voir.etymology_derivation: Latin vidēre lost its middle d: vedere → veoir → voir.

venir.etymology_derivation: Prefix it to build a whole family: revenir (come back), devenir (become), prévenir (warn).

tenir.etymology_derivation: Conjugates exactly like venir (je tiens, je viens).

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
